M1_teacher_talk_ratio.explanation: Share of *spoken* time held by the teacher. Non-speech is excluded on purpose, so hands-on noise does not dilute it.
M1_teacher_talk_ratio.interpretation: Reported only when the teacher/student split is separable; below that it is withheld rather than guessed. Observed average in conventional classrooms is about 61% teacher talk. A hands-on maker session should sit below 40%; above 70% the activity has become a lecture.

M2_student_participation.explanation: Student turns per child per hour, normalised by the headcount their own app recorded. 8 students and 27 students cannot be compared on raw turn counts.
M2_student_participation.interpretation: Depends on the speaker split, so it is withheld when that split is a guess. High student talk time with a low value here is the classic sign that two or three confident children are doing all the talking.

M3_interaction_density.explanation: How often the floor changes hands. Needs no transcript at all, so it survives audio the ASR cannot read.
M3_interaction_density.interpretation: Depends on the speaker split. High means genuine back-and-forth. Low with a high talk ratio is a monologue; low with a low talk ratio is unstructured activity with no teacher check-ins.

M4_longest_teacher_stretch.formula: max(continuous teacher speech, merging pauses under 3s)
M4_longest_teacher_stretch.explanation: The longest the teacher talked without stopping. The most concrete number on the page, and the easiest to picture changing.
M4_longest_teacher_stretch.interpretation: Depends on the speaker split. In a 60-minute maker session anything over about five minutes means the making stopped.

M5_wait_time_1.explanation: Mary Budd Rowe's wait time: the pause after a question before a student answers. Measured from raw diarization turns, which keep the real silences - the segment timeline tiles exactly, so gaps there are always zero. Depends on reading questions out of the transcript, so it is the first metric to become unreliable in a noisy room.
M5_wait_time_1.interpretation: Below 1s, answers are short and students say 'I don't know'. At 3s or more, responses get longer, more correct, and more students join in. It is the single most replicated finding in this field. Measured from 19 question-answer pairs.

M7_teacher_questions.formula: count(teacher turns whose transcript reads as a question)
M7_teacher_questions.explanation: Every question the teacher asked, answered or not. The unanswered ones are the point: M5 can only see a question a student replied to, so a room where nobody answers looks the same there as a room where nobody was asked. Detection is lexical - a Hindi interrogative or a question mark - because Hindi does not invert word order for questions, so there is little else to go on without prosody.
M7_teacher_questions.interpretation: About 35 per hour on this recording. Asking more is not automatically better - read it with M8, which says how many of them a student actually answered. A high count here with a low share there is a teacher questioning into silence.

M8_student_responses.formula: count(questions answered by a student within 15s)
M8_student_responses.explanation: How many of those questions a student actually took up. A student already talking as the question lands counts - that is an answer with no wait, not a missing one. A student who speaks a minute later does not; that is the next exchange, not this one.
M8_student_responses.interpretation: Students answered 22 of 22 questions (100%). A low share with a high question count is the signature of rhetorical questions the teacher answers herself - the most common thing this measurement finds.
